blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Hydrocarbons), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the classification of hydrocarbons into aliphatic and aromatic classes. Name the families of aliphatic hydrocarbons with one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydrocarbons are organic compounds of only carbon and hydrogen, found abundantly in petroleum and natural gas. They are broadly divided into two classes.

1. Aliphatic hydrocarbons: compounds that are not aromatic. They may be open chain or cyclic, saturated or unsaturated.
• Alkanes: acyclic, saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, e.g. ethane CH₃–CH₃.
• Cycloalkanes: cyclic, saturated, e.g. cyclohexane.
• Alkenes: acyclic, unsaturated (C=C), e.g. ethene CH₂=CH₂.
• Alkynes: acyclic, unsaturated (triple bond).

2. Aromatic hydrocarbons: a special class of cyclic hydrocarbons with a high carbon to hydrogen ratio, based on benzene (C₆H₆) or resembling compounds. Benzene is the basic aromatic compound; toluene and phenol are its derivatives. The name comes from the Greek 'aroma' (fragrant), as these compounds have a characteristic odour.

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbons are broadly divided into two classes that is aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons.

blocks.prompt: 2 What is an alkyl group? How are alkyl groups named? Write the alkyl groups that can be derived from propane and butane with their common and IUPAC names. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alkyl group: what we obtain after the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane. It is named by replacing -ane of the alkane with -yl: methane CH₄ → methyl CH₃– (Me–); ethane → ethyl CH₃CH₂– (Et–).

For alkanes with more than two carbon atoms more than one alkyl group can be derived, depending on which hydrogen is removed (Table 11.3):

book_ref.quote: What we obtain after the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane is called an alkyl group.

blocks.prompt: 3 State and explain the first four IUPAC rules for naming branched-chain alkanes, giving an example for each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Rule 1: Locate the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; it determines the parent name. It may be bent in the formula. E.g. CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ has a five-carbon chain: a pentane.

Rule 2: Number the longest chain beginning from the end nearest to the substituent. In the example above, numbering from the left puts CH₃ on C-2 (not C-4).

Rule 3: Use these numbers to show the location of the substituent. The substituent, preceded by its number, is placed first and the parent name last: 2-methylpentane; similarly 3-methylheptane and 2-methylhexane.

Rule 4: When two or more substituents are present, give each a number for its location on the longest chain, and list them alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), e.g. 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane; CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH(C₂H₅)–CH₂–CH₃ is 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane.

book_ref.quote: Branched chain alkanes are named according to the following rules.

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain the IUPAC rules for naming alkanes that (i) have two substituents on the same carbon, (ii) have identical substituents, (iii) have two competing chains of equal length, and (iv) branch at equal distances from both ends. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Rule 5: when two substituents are on the same carbon atom, use that number twice, e.g. 3-ethyl-3-methylhexane; CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH₃ is 3,3-dimethylpentane.

(ii) Rule 6: when two or more substituents are identical, show this by the prefixes di, tri, tetra and so on, and make certain each substituent has a number: 2,3-dimethylbutane, 2,3,4-trimethylpentane, 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane. Multiplying prefixes are ignored in alphabetical order.

(iii) Rule 7: when two chains of equal length compete for the parent chain, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents, e.g. 2,3,5-trimethyl-4-propylheptane.

(iv) Rule 8: when branching first occurs at an equal distance from either end, choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference, e.g. 2,3,5-trimethylhexane (not 2,4,5-).

book_ref.quote: Application of these six rules allows us to name most of the alkanes that we shall encounter.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the shapes of alkanes and cycloalkanes. How are cycloalkanes named? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alkanes: the carbon atom in an alkane has four sp³ hybridized orbitals and forms four single (σ) bonds with surrounding carbon and hydrogen atoms, equidistant from each other. The four bonding pairs repel each other equally, giving a tetrahedral shape around each carbon with bond angles of 109.5° and a C–C bond length of 1.54 Å (methane and ethane, Figure 11.4). Shapes are shown with ball and stick formulae (Table 11.4).

Cycloalkanes: the carbon atoms are arranged in the form of a ring. They are saturated: all ring carbons are singly bonded to other atoms. Their formula is CₙH₂ₙ, e.g. cyclopropane C₃H₆, cyclobutane C₄H₈, cyclopentane C₅H₁₀ (Table 11.5).

Naming: attach the prefix cyclo to the name of the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms, e.g. a six-carbon ring is cyclohexane.

book_ref.quote: Alkane molecules have a tetrahedral shape around carbon atoms.

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the physical properties of alkanes: physical state, colour and odour, solubility, and the trend in boiling points including the effect of branching. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Physical state: alkanes with up to four carbon atoms are gases; pentane to heptadecane (C₅ to C₁₇) are liquids; C₁₈ onwards are waxy solids.

2. Colour and odour: all are colourless and odourless.

3. Solubility: alkanes are non-polar or very weakly polar, so they are insoluble in polar solvents like water but soluble in non-polar solvents such as hexane, benzene and ether. Solubility decreases with increasing molecular mass.

4. Boiling points and other constants: boiling points, melting points and density increase with the number of carbon atoms. Branched-chain alkanes boil lower than their normal-chain isomers: butane boils at -0.50 °C, but its branched isomer 2-methylpropane (isobutane) at -11.7 °C.

book_ref.quote: Their physical constants, e.g. boiling points, melting points, density, etc increase with the increase in number of carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 7 What is a reaction mechanism? Describe the two modes of breaking a covalent bond, naming the species formed in each, with an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reaction mechanism: the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction. Organic reactions involve breaking of covalent bonds, which can happen in two ways.

(a) Homolytic fission: the covalent bond breaks evenly; each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, producing free radicals (Figure 11.5). Example: Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl• (in UV light). A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron; it is extremely reactive because unpaired electrons tend to become paired.

(b) Heterolytic fission: the bond breaks so that the shared pair of electrons is gained by one atom only, producing oppositely charged ions. Example: R₃C–Cl → R₃C⁺ + Cl⁻, a carbocation and a chloride ion (Figure 11.6). It is shown by full curly arrows in mechanisms.

book_ref.quote: Like all chemical reactions, organic reactions involve the breaking of chemical bonds.

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain why alkanes are called paraffins and why they are unreactive towards polar reagents under ordinary conditions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Paraffins: from Latin parum = little and affins = affinity. Alkanes are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents under ordinary conditions.

1. Non-polarity of bonds: the electronegativities of carbon (2.5) and hydrogen (2.1) differ by only 0.4, so the bonding electrons in C–H and C–C bonds are almost equally shared. The bonds are almost non-polar, so polar reagents (which attack charged or partially charged sites) find nothing to attack.

2. Inertness of the sigma bond: alkanes contain only σ bonds. In a σ bond the electrons are very tightly held between the nuclei, making it very stable; a lot of energy is needed to break it.

Hence alkanes react only under high temperature or suitable conditions, e.g. combustion, cracking and free radical substitution in light.

book_ref.quote: The lack of reactivity of alkanes under normal conditions may be explained on the basis of the non-polarity of the bonds forming them.

blocks.prompt: 9 Discuss the halogenation of alkanes with respect to: the conditions needed, the effect of the nature of the halogen, the successive products from methane, and the dependence on the amount of halogen. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Halogenation is the substitution of hydrogen atoms of an alkane by halogen atoms through highly reactive free radicals.

1. Conditions: alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in sunlight or UV light.

2. Nature of halogen: order of reactivity F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Fluorine reacts highly violently, giving a mixture of carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid. Iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible.

3. Successive products from methane:
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (chloromethane)
CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl (dichloromethane)
CH₂Cl₂ + Cl₂ → CHCl₃ + HCl (trichloromethane, chloroform)
CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl (tetrachloromethane, carbon tetrachloride)

4. Amount of halogen: the extent of halogenation depends upon the amount of halogen used; the more chlorine at the start, the greater the proportion of chlorine atoms in the chloroalkanes formed. Haloalkanes are anaesthetic and toxic, so their use as lab solvents is strictly monitored.

book_ref.quote: Alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in the presence of sunlight or UV light resulting in the successive replacement of hydrogen atoms with halogens.

blocks.prompt: 10 Write the free radical mechanism for the chlorination of ethane in UV light, showing all three possible termination steps. Which product shows that the mechanism goes through free radicals? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Overall: CH₃–CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃–CH₂Cl + HCl (UV light).

(i) Initiation: the Cl–Cl bond breaks homolytically using energy from UV light:
Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•

(ii) Propagation: the radicals attack the alkane, generating more free radicals:
CH₃–CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃–CH₂• + HCl
CH₃–CH₂• + Cl–Cl → CH₃–CH₂Cl + Cl•
The new Cl• repeats the cycle; repetition gives a mixture of chloroethanes.

(iii) Termination: two free radicals combine to form a product:
CH₃–CH₂• + Cl• → CH₃–CH₂Cl
Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
CH₃–CH₂• + •CH₂–CH₃ → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (butane)

Evidence: butane has double the carbon atoms of ethane and can form only when two ethyl radicals merge. This termination is rare, so butane forms in traces, but its presence is evidence of the free radical substitution mechanism.

book_ref.quote: Halogenation involves the following three steps.

blocks.prompt: 11 State the IUPAC rules for naming alkenes. Illustrate them by naming CH₃–CH₂–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ and (CH₃)₂CH–CH=CH₂. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C; they have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkanes.

Rule 1: Select the longest continuous chain that contains the C=C as the parent chain, and change the ending of the alkane of identical length from -ane to -ene.
Rule 2: Number the chain so as to include both carbon atoms of the double bond, beginning from the end nearer to the double bond.
Rule 3: Show the location of the double bond by the number of its first carbon as a prefix (1-butene, 1-pentene).
Rule 4: Show the locations of substituents by the numbers of the carbons to which they are attached (2-methyl-2-butene).
Rule 5: With more than one double bond the names are alkadienes (two), alkatrienes (three) and so on.

Examples: CH₃–CH₂–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃: seven-carbon chain; numbering from the left end (nearer to C=C) puts the double bond at C-3: 3-heptene.
(CH₃)₂CH–CH=CH₂: the longest chain with C=C has four carbons; numbering from CH₂= puts the double bond at C-1 and CH₃ at C-3: 3-methyl-1-butene.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC rules for naming alkenes are similar in many respects to those for naming alkanes.

blocks.prompt: 12 What are elimination reactions? Explain how concentrated sulphuric acid converts ethanol into ethene, writing the equations for both stages, and state the role of the acid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Elimination reactions: alkenes are prepared by removing small atoms (H, OH, X) from adjacent carbon atoms of a saturated compound, creating a double bond between the carbons. A small molecule such as H₂O or HCl is removed from adjacent carbons.

Dehydration of ethanol: ethanol is heated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 180°C; a water molecule is removed from the alcohol molecule. Overall:
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (H₂SO₄, heat)

Stage 1: ethyl hydrogen sulphate is formed:
CH₃–CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃–CH₂–OSO₃H + H₂O (180°C)

Stage 2: ethyl hydrogen sulphate decomposes on heating to give ethene:
CH₃–CH₂OSO₃H → H₂C=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ (heat)

Role of H₂SO₄: it removes the water, forming the intermediate ethyl hydrogen sulphate, and is given back in stage 2.

book_ref.quote: Alkenes are prepared by the removal of small atoms (H,OH,X) from the adjacent carbon atoms of the saturated compounds

blocks.prompt: 13 Compare alkanes and alkenes with respect to general formula, hybridization and shape, type of bonds, polarity, reactivity and the typical reactions they undergo. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are saturated and inert; alkenes are unsaturated, contain a π bond and are reactive.

book_ref.quote: Unlike alkanes, they show weakly polar properties because of sp² hybridization

rows: Unsaturated; two H less than the alkane (one C=C).
Double-bond carbons sp²; trigonal planar, about 120°.
σ bonds plus one π bond in C=C.
Weakly polar because of sp² hybridization.
Inert towards polar reagents under ordinary conditions.
Reactive; loosely held π electrons are exposed to electrophiles.
Electrophilic addition; also oxidation, combustion, polymerization.
Burn; C₁-C₄ gases, colourless and odourless.
Characteristic smell; burn with a luminous flame; C₂-C₄ gases.

blocks.prompt: 14 Explain the structure of ethene on the basis of sp² hybridization, describing the formation of the σ and π bonds and the shape of the molecule. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hybridization: ethene (C₂H₄) is the simplest alkene. Each carbon mixes its 2s orbital with two 2p orbitals to form three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals lying in one plane; one unhybrid p-orbital is left, perpendicular (90°) to this plane (Figure 11.8).

σ bonds: each carbon uses two sp² orbitals to form two C–H σ bonds with the 1s orbitals of hydrogen. The remaining sp² orbital on each carbon forms the C–C σ bond by linear overlap (Figure 11.9).

π bond: the unhybrid p-orbitals of the two carbons are parallel and overlap laterally to form the π bond, so C=C consists of one σ and one π bond.

Shape: sp² gives a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon with bond angles of about 120°. The two double-bond carbons and the four atoms attached to them lie in the same plane, so ethene is a planar molecule (Figure 11.10).

book_ref.quote: In ethene, each carbon uses two sp² orbitals to form two C–H bonds each.

blocks.prompt: 15 Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes and why they undergo electrophilic addition. Define electrophile and nucleophile, and explain why the reactions of alkenes depend on carbocations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Weak π bond: in a π bond the probability of finding the electrons is away from the line joining the two nuclei, so π electrons are less firmly held. A π bond is weak compared with a σ bond and breaks comparatively easily during a reaction. Alkanes have only strong σ bonds.

2. Exposed π electrons: the loosely held π electrons are exposed to attack by electrophilic reagents, so alkenes undergo electrophilic addition very easily.

3. Definitions: an electrophile (E⁺) is a species that acts as an electron pair acceptor. A nucleophile (Nu:⁻) is a species that acts as a donor of a pair of electrons. Alkenes act as nucleophiles because they contain π electrons.

4. Carbocations: when the π electrons attack an electrophile, a carbocation intermediate forms; the reactions of alkenes mostly proceed through carbocations, so their stability decides the product.

book_ref.quote: Moreover, the loosely held π-electrons are more exposed to attack by the electrophilic reagents.

blocks.prompt: 16 What is a carbocation? Classify carbocations with examples and explain, using the inductive effect of alkyl groups, the order of their stability. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Carbocation: an alkyl group with a single positive charge on one of its carbon atoms. Because of this positive charge it is an electrophile.

Classification (by the carbons bonded to the positive carbon):
• Methyl carbocation, bonded to H only: CH₃⁺
• Primary (1°), bonded to one carbon: CH₃CH₂⁺
• Secondary (2°), bonded to two carbons: (CH₃)₂CH⁺
• Tertiary (3°), bonded to three carbons: (CH₃)₃C⁺

Inductive effect: the polarization of a σ bond due to the electron withdrawing or donating effect of adjacent groups. Alkyl groups are slightly electron donating (+I). The alkyl groups attached to the positive carbon push electrons towards it (shown by arrowheads on the bonds), so the carbocation becomes less positive and energetically more stable.

Order: stability increases with the number of alkyl groups: (CH₃)₃C⁺ > (CH₃)₂CH⁺ > CH₃CH₂⁺ > CH₃⁺. The tertiary carbocation, with three electron-donating alkyl groups, is the most stable (Figure 11.11).

book_ref.quote: The inductive effect of alkyl groups plays an important role in the stability of carbocation.

blocks.prompt: 17 Define the inductive effect. Explain the positive and negative inductive effects with examples, and describe the polarization of the σ bonds in a chloroalkane. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: the polarization of a σ bond due to the electron withdrawing or electron donating effect of adjacent groups or atoms is the inductive effect.

Positive inductive effect (+I): shown by electron donating species, e.g. alkyl groups. Alkyl groups attached to a positive carbon push electrons towards it and stabilize carbocations; the more alkyl groups, the more stable the carbocation.

Negative inductive effect (-I): shown by electron withdrawing groups, e.g. a halogen atom. The halogen withdraws the bonded electrons from carbon.

Polarization in a chloroalkane C₂–C₁–Cl (Figure 11.12): chlorine pulls the electrons of the C₁–Cl bond, so chlorine holds a partial negative charge and C₁ becomes partial positive (δ⁺). C₁ in turn pulls electrons from the C₂–C₁ bond, so C₂ carries a smaller positive charge (δδ⁺). A permanent dipole arises in the molecule; the effect weakens along the chain.

book_ref.quote: Halogen withdraws bonded electrons from carbon to carbon bond and thus displays negative inductive effect.

blocks.prompt: 18 How is bromine used to test for unsaturation? Describe the three-step mechanism of the addition of bromine to ethene. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Test: when bromine (red-brown) is added to ethene in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride, its reddish brown colour is discharged at once. The reaction is used to identify the unsaturation of an organic compound.
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → Br–CH₂–CH₂–Br

Mechanism (Figure 11.14):
Step (i) Polarization of Br₂: Br₂ is non-polar, but as it approaches the C=C, the high electron density of the double bond repels the Br–Br electron pair away from the nearer Br atom. That Br becomes slightly positive (Brᵟ⁺–Brᵟ⁻) and acts as the electrophile.

Step (ii) Electrophilic attack: the π electrons of the double bond attack the δ⁺ bromine, which accepts the electron pair from C=C. The Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically, giving Br⁻ and a highly reactive carbocation intermediate, CH₂Br–CH₂⁺.

Step (iii) Nucleophilic attack: the carbocation reacts with Br⁻ (nucleophile) to give the product Br–CH₂–CH₂–Br.

book_ref.quote: The above reaction proceeds through a three–steps mechanism as given below:

blocks.prompt: 19 Using carbocation stability, explain why HBr adds to 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, to give mainly 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Write the steps of the mechanism. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
2-Methylpropene is an unsymmetrical alkene, so two products are theoretically possible. Markovnikov's rule: when a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part of the reagent attaches to the double-bonded carbon bearing fewer hydrogens.

Step 1 (electrophilic attack): H–Br is polar (Hᵟ⁺–Brᵟ⁻). The π electrons of C=C attack the partial positive H; HBr breaks heterolytically giving Br⁻. Two carbocations are possible:
(a) H adds to CH₂ (the carbon with more hydrogens): (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₃, i.e. (CH₃)₃C⁺, a tertiary (3°) carbocation.
(b) H adds to the other carbon: (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂⁺, a primary (1°) carbocation.

Stability: the 3° carbocation has three electron-donating (+I) alkyl groups on the positive carbon, so it is far more stable and forms mainly.

Step 2 (nucleophilic attack): Br⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the 3° carbocation:
(CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻ → (CH₃)₃C–Br, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (major).
Attack on the 1° carbocation gives the minor product (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂Br, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. Br has gone to the carbon with fewer hydrogens, as the rule states.

book_ref.quote: Markovnikov’s Rule is applicable for addition reactions in alkenes.

blocks.prompt: 20 Describe the hydrogenation, hydration and halohydration of ethene, giving the conditions, equations and products, and one industrial use of hydrogenation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Hydrogenation: addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene in the presence of a Ni/Pt catalyst at 250-300 °C, forming a saturated compound.
H₂C=CH₂ + H₂ → H₃C–CH₃ (Ni, 250-300 °C)
Industrial use: vegetable oil is converted into margarine (Banaspati ghee): Oil + H₂ → Margarine (Ni).

2. Hydration: gaseous alkenes react with steam at high temperature and pressure with concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst to form alcohols.
H₂C=CH₂ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (H₂SO₄)
As in hydrohalogenation, the alkene forms a carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked to give the alcohol.

3. Halohydration: an alkene reacts with a halogen (bromine or chlorine) in the presence of water to form a halohydrin. Br and OH add to the two carbons of the double bond:
H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → Br–CH₂–CH₂–OH + HBr
Product: 2-bromoethanol (ethylene bromohydrin); with chlorine a chlorohydrin forms.

book_ref.quote: Gaseous alkenes react with steam at high temperature and pressure in the presence of concentrated acid (H₂SO₄) as the catalyst to form alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 21 What is addition polymerization? Explain how the bonding changes when ethene and chloroethene polymerize, and how the repeating unit of a poly(alkene) is deduced from its monomer. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Polymerization: the formation of extremely long molecules (polymers) from small reactive molecules (monomers) that join together.

Addition polymerization: many monomers containing at least one C=C form long polymer chains as the only product. It is the basis of the plastics industry.

Change in bonding: as in other addition reactions, the π bond of each C=C breaks and the monomers link together through new C–C single bonds.
n CH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ  poly(ethene)
n CH₂=CHCl → [–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ  PVC (every second carbon carries Cl)

Repeating unit: the smallest group of atoms that, connected one after another, makes up the polymer chain; it is shown in square brackets. For a poly(alkene) made of one monomer, the repeating unit is the same as the monomer except that the C=C becomes a C–C single bond.

Uses: polyethylene is used in bags, bottles and packaging; PVC is used for articles such as ball pens.

book_ref.quote: A polymer is a long-chain molecule that is made up of many repeating units.

blocks.prompt: 22 What are conjugated dienes? Explain the delocalization of π electrons in them, give two examples and state their industrial importance. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Diene: a molecule containing two double bonds between carbon atoms. In a conjugated diene the double bonds in the carbon chain are separated by a single bond.

Delocalization: the adjacent double bonds allow overlap of p-orbitals on three or more adjacent atoms. This overlap delocalizes the π electrons, so the π-bond overlap extends over the entire system. Delocalization can stabilize the molecule and affect its reactivity.

Examples:
CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂  but-1,3-diene (1,3-butadiene)
CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂  2-methylbut-1,3-diene (isoprene)

Importance: conjugated dienes such as 1,3-butadiene are used in the production of synthetic rubber; the conjugated structure allows polymerization into long chains that show rubber-like properties.

book_ref.quote: This overlap leads to a delocalization of electrons, which can stabilize the molecule and affect its reactivity.

blocks.prompt: 23 Define isomerism. Explain chain, position and functional group isomerism with one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Isomerism: two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural formulas and properties are isomers, and the phenomenon is isomerism. It is common for compounds with more than three carbon atoms; the number of isomers rises rapidly with carbon number (pentane has three). Structural isomerism arises from a difference in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule.

1. Chain isomerism: arises from a difference in the nature of the carbon chain.
Example (C₄H₁₀): CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (butane) and CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ (2-methylpropane).

2. Position isomerism: arises from a difference in the position of the same functional group on the carbon chain; the arrangement of carbon atoms stays the same.
Example (C₄H₈): CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₃ (but-1-ene) and CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ (but-2-ene); similarly 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

3. Functional group isomerism: same molecular formula but different functional groups.
Example (C₂H₆O): CH₃–CH₂–OH (ethanol, an alcohol) and CH₃–O–CH₃ (methoxymethane, an ether).

book_ref.quote: As the number of carbon atoms in a hydrocarbon increases, the number of possible isomers increase very rapidly.

blocks.prompt: 24 Explain metamerism and tautomerism with examples. Name the two types of stereoisomerism and state how stereoisomers differ from structural isomers. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Metamerism: arises from the unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group; the metamers belong to the same homologous series.
Ethers (C₄H₁₀O): CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃ (ethoxyethane, diethyl ether) and CH₃–O–CH₂CH₂CH₃ (methoxypropane).
Ketones (C₅H₁₀O): CH₃–CO–CH₂CH₂CH₃ (2-pentanone) and CH₃CH₂–CO–CH₂CH₃ (3-pentanone).

2. Tautomerism: arises from the shifting of a proton from one atom to another in the same molecule. It is commonly seen in amino acids, which exist as zwitterions formed when a proton shifts from the carboxylic acid end to the amine group.

3. Stereoisomerism: stereoisomers have the same structural formula but differ in the positions of identical groups in space (structural isomers differ in their structural formulas). Two types: geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism and optical isomerism; these are covered in the Class 12 syllabus.

book_ref.quote: This type of isomerism arises due to the unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group.

blocks.prompt: 25 What are organic redox reactions? Describe, with equations, the oxidation of organic compounds (combustion, ozonolysis, epoxidation, oxidation of a primary alcohol) and their reduction (hydrogenation and the use of reducing agents). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Organic redox reactions: oxidation-reduction reactions that involve organic compounds. They are characterized by the addition or removal of atoms/bonds. In organic oxidation oxygen is added or hydrogen removed; in organic reduction hydrogen is added or oxygen removed.

Oxidation:
• Combustion (reaction with oxygen): 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O (C₂H₆ + 7/2 O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O).
• Ozonolysis: oxidative cleavage of an alkene by ozone (O₃) via an ozonide, giving carbonyl compounds, e.g. C₂H₄ + O₃ → C₂H₄O₃ → 2CH₂O.
• Epoxidation: an alkene gives an epoxide with oxidizing agents such as molecular oxygen and metal catalysts (ethene → ethylene oxide).
• Primary alcohol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives a carboxylic acid: C₂H₅OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O.

Reduction:
• Hydrogenation of C=C: H₂C=CH₂ + H–H → H₃C–CH₃ (Pt).
• Reducing agents in organic synthesis: LiAlH₄, NaBH₄, Sn + conc. HCl, e.g. CH₃–CHO + 2[H] → CH₃–CH₂–OH (LiAlH₄, heat). Reductions of nitriles and amides to amines, carboxylic acids to primary alcohols and nitrobenzene to phenylamine are studied in Class 12.

book_ref.quote: Oxidation-Reduction reactions that involve organic compounds are called organic redox reactions.
